metadata.description: Validates expertise in designing, building, and managing data processing systems on AWS, including data pipelines, data lakes, and analytics solutions.

questions.title: Real-Time Streaming Data Ingestion
questions.scenario: A retail company wants to capture clickstream data from their e-commerce website in real-time. The data should be processed within seconds and made available for real-time analytics dashboards. Peak traffic can reach 100,000 events per second during flash sales.
questions.questionText: Which AWS service combination provides the most cost-effective solution for ingesting and processing this high-volume streaming data?

choices.text: Amazon MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka) with Kafka Streams
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose with direct S3 delivery
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with AWS Lambda consumers
Amazon SQS with EC2-based consumers

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider which service provides native real-time processing with automatic scaling for variable workloads.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with Lambda consumers is ideal for this scenario. Kinesis Data Streams can handle 100,000+ records per second with on-demand capacity mode. Lambda consumers process data in near real-time (sub-second latency) and scale automatically with the stream. This combination is cost-effective because you pay only for actual usage. MSK requires more management overhead and fixed capacity. Kinesis Firehose has minimum 60-second buffering, not suitable for sub-second requirements. SQS is not designed for ordered streaming analytics.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Kinesis Data Streams on-demand mode automatically scales from thousands to millions of records per second
  • Lambda Enhanced Fan-Out provides dedicated throughput of 2 MB/second per consumer
  • Kinesis processes records in order within each shard, essential for clickstream analysis
  • Lambda concurrent executions scale with number of shards for parallel processing
  • Consider Kinesis Data Analytics for complex real-time SQL or Apache Flink processing

questions.title: Data Lake Storage Architecture
questions.scenario: A media company stores 500 TB of video metadata and user interaction logs. Analytics teams run daily batch queries analyzing viewing patterns, while data scientists need ad-hoc queries for ML feature engineering. Query patterns vary significantly, with some queries scanning entire datasets and others targeting specific date ranges.
questions.questionText: Which storage format and partitioning strategy optimizes query performance and cost for this data lake?

choices.text: Store data in CSV format partitioned by video_id
Store data in Apache Avro format partitioned by user_id
Store data in JSON format with no partitioning for flexibility
Store data in Apache Parquet format partitioned by date with Snappy compression

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What type of storage format best supports queries that read a few columns across many rows?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Apache Parquet with date partitioning and Snappy compression is optimal for this scenario. Parquet is a columnar format that enables efficient column pruning and predicate pushdown, reducing data scanned. Date partitioning aligns with daily batch queries and time-range ad-hoc queries, enabling partition pruning. Snappy compression provides a good balance between compression ratio and query speed. CSV lacks columnar benefits, JSON is inefficient for analytics, and user_id partitioning would create too many small partitions and not align with query patterns.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Parquet stores data in row groups with column chunks, enabling parallel column reads
  • Parquet min/max statistics in footer enable predicate pushdown without reading data
  • Date partitioning creates S3 prefixes like s3://bucket/year=2024/month=01/day=15/
  • Athena and Redshift Spectrum leverage partition pruning to skip irrelevant partitions
  • Consider Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake for ACID transactions and time travel capabilities

questions.title: CDC Pipeline Architecture
questions.scenario: A financial services company needs to replicate transaction data from an on-premises Oracle database to AWS for analytics. The source database processes 50,000 transactions per hour and requires near real-time replication with minimal impact on source database performance. Data must be available in both a data warehouse and a data lake.
questions.questionText: Which architecture provides the most efficient change data capture (CDC) pipeline?

choices.text: Custom application reading Oracle redo logs and writing to SQS
AWS DMS with CDC directly to both Redshift and S3 simultaneously
AWS DMS with CDC to Kinesis Data Streams, then Lambda to write to Redshift and S3
Scheduled full table exports using AWS DMS every 15 minutes

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider how to efficiently fan out CDC events to multiple destinations while maintaining order.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: AWS DMS with CDC to Kinesis Data Streams provides the best architecture. DMS reads Oracle redo logs with minimal source impact. Kinesis acts as a durable buffer enabling multiple consumers. Lambda can transform and route events to both Redshift and S3 independently. This decouples producers from consumers and handles backpressure gracefully. Direct DMS to multiple targets increases source load and complexity. Custom redo log parsing is error-prone. Full exports every 15 minutes create high latency and source load.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• DMS uses Oracle LogMiner or Binary Reader for low-impact CDC from redo logs
  • Kinesis preserves transaction ordering within shards using primary key as partition key
  • Consider Kinesis Data Firehose for S3 delivery with automatic batching and Parquet conversion
  • Use Redshift Streaming Ingestion for sub-second latency to Redshift from Kinesis
  • DMS validation feature ensures data integrity between source and target

questions.title: ETL Workflow Orchestration
questions.scenario: A healthcare analytics company runs 200+ daily ETL jobs with complex dependencies. Jobs include Glue ETL, EMR Spark jobs, Redshift stored procedures, and Lambda functions. Some job chains take 6 hours to complete and require automatic retry logic with exponential backoff. The team needs visibility into job status and alerting on failures.
questions.questionText: Which orchestration solution best meets these requirements?

choices.text: AWS Glue Workflows with triggers and CloudWatch Events
Amazon MWAA (Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow)
AWS Step Functions with state machines
Cron jobs on EC2 instances with custom dependency tracking

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: With 200+ jobs spanning multiple AWS compute services, what kind of orchestration model handles cross-service dependencies best?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Amazon MWAA (Managed Airflow) is ideal for complex ETL orchestration. Airflow provides DAG-based dependency management, native operators for Glue, EMR, Redshift, and Lambda, built-in retry with exponential backoff, and a web UI for monitoring. With 200+ jobs and 6-hour chains, Airflow's scheduling and dependency features are essential. Glue Workflows only orchestrate Glue jobs. Step Functions can orchestrate but DAG definition and monitoring are less intuitive for ETL teams. EC2 cron lacks dependency management and reliability.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• MWAA uses Airflow's Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) model for dependency definition
  • Airflow sensors enable waiting for external events like S3 file arrival
  • MWAA integrates with Secrets Manager for secure credential management
  • Task-level retry configuration with max_retries and retry_delay parameters
  • CloudWatch integration provides metrics and log aggregation for DAG runs

questions.title: Data Lake Security and Governance
questions.scenario: A pharmaceutical company is building a data lake containing clinical trial data. Different research teams need access to specific datasets based on their projects. Some columns contain personally identifiable information (PII) that should be masked for certain users. All data access must be audited for regulatory compliance.
questions.questionText: Which service combination provides the most comprehensive data governance solution?

choices.text: Amazon Macie for data discovery with manual access controls
Glue Data Catalog with resource-based policies
AWS Lake Formation with column-level security and data filters
S3 bucket policies with IAM roles per team

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: What granularity of access control does PII masking for specific users require — bucket, table, or finer?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: AWS Lake Formation provides comprehensive data lake governance. It offers column-level security to restrict PII access, data filters for row-level security, centralized permission management across Glue, Athena, and Redshift Spectrum, and CloudTrail integration for audit logging. Lake Formation simplifies governance compared to managing individual S3 and IAM policies. S3 bucket policies lack column-level control. Glue Data Catalog alone doesn't provide column masking. Macie discovers sensitive data but doesn't control access.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Lake Formation Tag-Based Access Control (LF-TBAC) enables attribute-based permissions
  • Data filters create virtual views that mask or exclude rows based on user context
  • Lake Formation governed tables provide ACID transactions for data lakes
  • Cross-account data sharing with Lake Formation maintains governance controls
  • Integration with AWS RAM enables sharing data catalog resources across accounts

questions.title: Batch Data Ingestion from Multiple Sources
questions.scenario: A logistics company needs to ingest daily CSV files from 50 different suppliers. Files arrive at various times throughout the day in different S3 buckets. Each file needs validation, format standardization, and loading into a central data warehouse. The team wants a serverless solution with minimal operational overhead.
questions.questionText: Which approach provides the most efficient batch ingestion pipeline?

choices.text: EMR cluster running continuous Spark Streaming jobs
S3 event notifications triggering AWS Glue ETL jobs for each file
AWS Data Pipeline with scheduled activities
Scheduled Lambda functions polling each S3 bucket hourly

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider event-driven architecture for processing files as they arrive without polling overhead.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: S3 event notifications triggering Glue ETL jobs provides an efficient serverless solution. When files land in S3, events automatically trigger Glue jobs for validation and transformation. Glue is serverless, scales automatically, and integrates with the Glue Data Catalog for schema management. This event-driven approach processes files immediately without polling. Lambda polling adds complexity and cost. Data Pipeline is being deprecated. EMR requires cluster management and is overkill for batch CSV processing.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Use S3 Event Notifications with EventBridge for advanced filtering and routing
  • Glue crawlers can automatically infer schemas from incoming CSV files
  • Glue job bookmarks track processed files to prevent reprocessing
  • Consider Glue workflows to chain validation, transformation, and loading jobs
  • Glue DataBrew provides visual data preparation for non-technical users

questions.title: Data Warehouse Optimization
questions.scenario: A retail analytics team uses Amazon Redshift with 10 TB of sales data. Queries analyzing recent 90-day data run frequently and need sub-second response times. Historical queries beyond 90 days run occasionally for annual reports. Storage costs are a concern, and the team wants to optimize both performance and cost.
questions.questionText: Which Redshift configuration optimizes this workload pattern?

choices.text: Use RA3 nodes with managed storage and Redshift Spectrum for historical data in S3
Use DC2 nodes with all data stored locally
Use Redshift Serverless for all queries
Store all data in S3 and use only Redshift Spectrum

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider separating hot and cold data tiers for cost optimization while maintaining performance.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: RA3 nodes with managed storage and Redshift Spectrum provide optimal cost-performance balance. RA3 nodes automatically tier frequently accessed data to fast local SSD cache while storing bulk data in S3-backed managed storage. Recent 90-day hot data stays cached for sub-second queries. Historical data beyond 90 days can be stored in S3 and queried via Spectrum, reducing storage costs significantly. DC2 local storage is expensive at scale. Serverless may have cold start latency. Spectrum-only lacks the performance for frequent queries.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• RA3 managed storage costs approximately $0.024/GB/month vs local SSD at higher cost
  • Automatic workload management (WLM) prioritizes short queries for interactive use
  • Materialized views can pre-aggregate common query patterns for faster response
  • AQUA (Advanced Query Accelerator) pushes filtering to storage layer on RA3
  • Data sharing enables separating compute and storage across Redshift clusters

questions.title: Data Quality Monitoring
questions.scenario: An insurance company processes claims data through multiple ETL stages. Data quality issues in upstream systems have caused incorrect analytics reports. The team needs automated data quality checks that validate completeness, accuracy, and freshness at each pipeline stage, with alerting when issues are detected.
questions.questionText: Which approach provides comprehensive automated data quality monitoring?

choices.text: Custom SQL validation queries scheduled in Athena
AWS Glue Data Quality with rules defined in Glue ETL jobs
Amazon Macie for data classification and quality
CloudWatch custom metrics with manual threshold alerts

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Should quality checks run inside the pipeline or as a separate post-processing step? Think about where rules catch issues earliest.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: AWS Glue Data Quality provides native integration with Glue ETL jobs for automated quality checks. You define rules using Data Quality Definition Language (DQDL) for completeness, uniqueness, accuracy, and freshness validations. Rules run automatically during ETL execution with pass/fail results and detailed metrics. Failed quality checks can halt pipelines or trigger alerts via EventBridge and SNS. Custom SQL requires manual integration and lacks built-in alerting. Macie focuses on sensitive data discovery. CloudWatch metrics require custom instrumentation.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• DQDL supports rules like Completeness, Uniqueness, ColumnValues, and CustomSql
  • Glue Data Quality evaluates rules and generates quality scores (0-100%)
  • Integration with Glue Data Catalog enables quality metrics in data lineage
  • Anomaly detection rules identify statistical deviations from historical patterns
  • Quality results publish to CloudWatch for dashboards and trend analysis

questions.title: Data Encryption Architecture
questions.scenario: A government contractor must implement encryption for data at rest and in transit across their data platform. They require customer-managed encryption keys with annual rotation, separate keys for different data classifications, and the ability to audit all key usage. Data flows between S3, Redshift, and EMR.
questions.questionText: Which encryption architecture meets these requirements?

choices.text: AWS managed keys (SSE-S3) for all services with CloudTrail logging
Client-side encryption with keys stored in Secrets Manager
S3 bucket keys with default encryption only
AWS KMS customer managed keys (CMKs) with key policies and automatic rotation

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Who should control the encryption keys — the service, the customer, or a third party? What does that choice imply for auditing?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: AWS KMS with customer managed keys (CMKs) provides the required encryption architecture. CMKs support automatic annual rotation, key policies for access control, and complete CloudTrail audit logging of all key operations. Different CMKs can be created for each data classification (e.g., secret, confidential, public). S3, Redshift, and EMR all integrate natively with KMS for transparent encryption. SSE-S3 lacks customer control. Client-side encryption adds complexity. S3 bucket keys optimize cost but don't address multi-service requirements.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• KMS automatic key rotation creates new key material annually while retaining old material for decryption
  • Key policies define which IAM principals can use or manage each CMK
  • KMS grants provide temporary access to keys for specific services like EMR
  • Redshift uses envelope encryption with CMK protecting data encryption keys
  • CloudTrail logs every KMS API call including Encrypt, Decrypt, and GenerateDataKey

questions.title: IoT Data Ingestion at Scale
questions.scenario: An energy company monitors 500,000 smart meters that send readings every 15 minutes. Each reading includes meter ID, timestamp, energy consumption, and voltage metrics. Data must be stored for 7 years with the ability to run both real-time anomaly detection and historical trend analysis.
questions.questionText: Which architecture handles this IoT data ingestion and storage requirement?

choices.text: API Gateway with Lambda processing each meter reading individually
Direct MQTT to EC2 fleet with custom processing and RDS storage
AWS IoT Core to Kinesis Data Streams, with Kinesis Data Analytics for anomalies and Firehose to S3 for storage
AWS IoT Core directly to DynamoDB with DynamoDB Streams for processing

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The scenario needs both real-time anomaly detection and cheap long-term storage. How many layers does that require?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: AWS IoT Core to Kinesis provides optimal IoT data architecture. IoT Core handles MQTT connections from 500,000 devices with automatic scaling. Kinesis Data Streams buffers the 2 million readings per hour reliably. Kinesis Data Analytics (Apache Flink) enables real-time anomaly detection using statistical algorithms. Kinesis Data Firehose delivers data to S3 in Parquet format for cost-effective 7-year storage. This separates real-time processing from historical storage. EC2 fleet requires management. API Gateway has request limits. DynamoDB is expensive for 7-year retention at this scale.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• IoT Core rules engine can route messages to multiple destinations simultaneously
  • Kinesis Data Analytics supports tumbling, sliding, and session windows for aggregation
  • Firehose automatic Parquet conversion reduces storage costs by 80% vs JSON
  • S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves old data to cheaper storage classes
  • Consider Amazon Timestream for time-series specific queries and automatic tiering

questions.title: Data Lake Table Format Selection
questions.scenario: A financial services firm is modernizing their data lake. They need ACID transactions for concurrent writes, time travel for regulatory audits, schema evolution for changing requirements, and efficient upserts for slowly changing dimensions. The solution should work with Athena, EMR, and Redshift Spectrum.
questions.questionText: Which table format best addresses these requirements?

choices.text: Apache Iceberg tables in AWS Glue Data Catalog
Standard Parquet files with Hive-style partitioning
Delta Lake with custom metadata management
Apache ORC files with manual versioning

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The scenario demands ACID updates and time travel on a data lake. Which choices even support transactional semantics?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Apache Iceberg provides all required capabilities with excellent AWS integration. Iceberg supports ACID transactions through optimistic concurrency control, time travel via snapshot isolation for audit queries, schema evolution without rewriting data, and efficient merge-on-read for upserts. AWS Glue Data Catalog natively supports Iceberg metadata, enabling seamless access from Athena, EMR, and Redshift Spectrum. Standard Parquet lacks transactions and time travel. Delta Lake has limited AWS native support. ORC requires manual version management.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Iceberg maintains metadata in manifest files tracking all data files and their statistics
  • Time travel uses snapshot IDs: SELECT * FROM table FOR VERSION AS OF snapshot_id
  • Schema evolution supports add, drop, rename, and reorder columns without rewrite
  • Merge operations use copy-on-write or merge-on-read strategies based on workload
  • Iceberg compaction optimizes file sizes and removes deleted data from storage

questions.title: Schema Discovery and Management
questions.scenario: A media company receives data from content partners in various formats including JSON, CSV, and Parquet. New data sources are added monthly, and schemas frequently change. The analytics team needs to quickly discover schemas and query data using SQL without manual schema definition.
questions.questionText: Which service combination automates schema discovery and enables immediate SQL querying?

choices.text: Manual schema definition in Hive Metastore with EMR Hive
Amazon Macie for schema discovery with Redshift queries
AWS Glue Crawlers with Glue Data Catalog and Amazon Athena
Lambda functions parsing files and storing schemas in DynamoDB

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Thousands of datasets in mixed formats need schemas discovered automatically. Is manual definition realistic at that scale?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Glue Crawlers with Data Catalog and Athena provides automated schema discovery. Crawlers automatically infer schemas from JSON, CSV, Parquet, and other formats, storing metadata in the Glue Data Catalog. When schemas change, crawlers detect and update catalog entries. Athena immediately queries data using catalog schemas without data movement. This combination requires no manual schema definition and handles new sources automatically. Manual Hive schemas don't auto-update. Macie discovers sensitive data, not schemas. Custom Lambda adds complexity.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Crawlers use classifiers to identify data formats and infer column types
  • Schema versioning in Data Catalog tracks changes and enables compatibility checks
  • Custom classifiers handle proprietary formats using grok patterns or JSON paths
  • Crawler scheduling ensures schemas stay current with source data changes
  • Data Catalog APIs enable programmatic schema management and integration

questions.title: Cross-Account Data Sharing
questions.scenario: A conglomerate has separate AWS accounts for each business unit. The central analytics team needs to query data from all business units without copying data. Each business unit must retain control over their data and approve access requests. Data governance and audit trails must be maintained.
questions.questionText: Which approach enables secure cross-account data sharing with governance?

choices.text: Copy all data to a central S3 bucket with cross-account IAM roles
AWS DataSync scheduled copies between accounts
S3 bucket policies allowing cross-account access
AWS Lake Formation cross-account sharing with LF-Tags

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Does sharing data across accounts require copying it, or can permissions be granted in place? What about governance overhead?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: AWS Lake Formation cross-account sharing with LF-Tags enables governed data sharing. Business units register their data in Lake Formation and define access using LF-Tags (e.g., department=finance, sensitivity=confidential). The central team requests access, and business units grant permissions through Lake Formation. Data remains in original accounts with no copying. All access is logged via CloudTrail. LF-Tags enable attribute-based access control across accounts. Data copying wastes storage and creates sync issues. S3 bucket policies lack fine-grained governance. DataSync creates duplicate data.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Lake Formation uses AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) for cross-account sharing
  • LF-Tags enable policy-based access: grant access to all tables tagged department=sales
  • Named resources sharing allows granting access to specific databases and tables
  • Central governance account can coordinate permissions across the organization
  • Hybrid access mode enables gradual migration from IAM to Lake Formation permissions

questions.title: Real-Time Data Transformation
questions.scenario: A gaming company streams player events at 1 million events per second during peak hours. Events need real-time enrichment with player profile data from DynamoDB, aggregation into 1-minute windows for leaderboards, and anomaly detection for fraud. Latency must be under 5 seconds from event to insight.
questions.questionText: Which stream processing architecture meets these latency and throughput requirements?

choices.text: EMR Spark Structured Streaming with batch DynamoDB queries
Lambda functions consuming from Kinesis with DynamoDB lookups
Kinesis Data Analytics for Apache Flink with async I/O for DynamoDB enrichment
Kinesis Data Firehose with Lambda transformation

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Enriching each event from an external store while computing sliding-window aggregations — is a simple consumer enough, or do you need a full processing framework?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Kinesis Data Analytics for Apache Flink provides the required capabilities. Flink's async I/O enables non-blocking DynamoDB lookups during enrichment without reducing throughput. Native windowing operators support 1-minute tumbling windows for aggregations. Flink's CEP (Complex Event Processing) library enables pattern-based anomaly detection. With proper parallelism, Flink handles millions of events per second with sub-second latency. Lambda has concurrency limits at this scale. Spark Structured Streaming has higher latency. Firehose has minimum 60-second buffering.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Flink async I/O batches DynamoDB requests for efficient throughput during enrichment
  • Flink maintains exactly-once semantics with Kinesis checkpointing
  • Application autoscaling adjusts parallelism based on Kinesis shard count
  • Flink state backends (RocksDB) enable large state for sessionization and aggregation
  • Side outputs route anomalies to separate Kinesis streams for alerting

questions.title: Time-Series Data Architecture
questions.scenario: A manufacturing company collects sensor data from 10,000 machines across 50 factories. Each sensor reports metrics every second, generating 500 million data points daily. Engineers need to query recent data (last 7 days) with millisecond response times for dashboards and analyze historical trends over years for predictive maintenance models.
questions.questionText: Which storage architecture optimizes both real-time queries and historical analysis?

choices.text: Amazon RDS PostgreSQL with TimescaleDB extension
Single DynamoDB table with TTL for data expiration
Amazon Timestream with memory store for recent data and magnetic store for historical
Elasticsearch with index lifecycle management

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The data has a clear hot/cold pattern over time. Should you build tiering yourself or look for a storage engine designed for that access pattern?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Amazon Timestream is purpose-built for this time-series workload. The memory store provides millisecond query latency for recent data (configurable retention, e.g., 7 days). Data automatically moves to the magnetic store for cost-effective long-term retention. Built-in time-series functions (interpolation, smoothing, approximation) accelerate analytics. Automatic data lifecycle management eliminates manual tiering. Timestream handles 500M+ daily records with serverless scaling. DynamoDB requires complex design for time-series. RDS doesn't scale to this volume. Elasticsearch is expensive for long-term storage.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Memory store uses in-memory caching with SSD backing for sub-millisecond reads
  • Magnetic store uses columnar storage optimized for time-series aggregation queries
  • Scheduled queries pre-aggregate data for dashboard performance optimization
  • Multi-measure records reduce storage cost by grouping related measurements
  • Timestream integrates with Grafana for real-time visualization dashboards

questions.title: Data Pipeline Cost Optimization
questions.scenario: A SaaS company's data pipeline processes 50 TB daily using EMR clusters for Spark jobs. Current costs are $200,000/month. Jobs run during business hours with 80% of processing between 9 AM and 5 PM. Some jobs are latency-sensitive (30-minute SLA), while batch jobs can tolerate delays. The team wants to reduce costs by 40% without impacting SLAs.
questions.questionText: Which combination of strategies achieves the cost reduction target?

choices.text: Migrate all workloads to AWS Glue with standard workers
Use EMR Serverless for all workloads regardless of latency requirements
Use EMR on EKS with Spot instances for batch jobs, Graviton instances, and intelligent auto-scaling
Use EMR on EC2 with 100% On-Demand instances and larger cluster sizes

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider combining instance pricing strategies with right-sizing and auto-scaling based on workload characteristics.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: EMR on EKS with strategic optimizations achieves 40%+ cost reduction. Spot instances for batch jobs (which tolerate interruption) save 60-90% on compute. Graviton (ARM) instances provide 20% better price-performance. EKS enables fine-grained pod scaling and bin-packing efficiency. Intelligent auto-scaling matches capacity to the 9-5 peak pattern. Reserve On-Demand or Savings Plans for latency-sensitive SLA jobs. This combination optimizes each workload type appropriately. 100% On-Demand wastes money. Glue may not match EMR performance. Serverless has startup latency concerns for SLA jobs.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• EMR on EKS enables Kubernetes-native autoscaling with Karpenter for rapid scaling
  • Instance fleets diversify across multiple Spot pools for availability
  • Graviton3 processors optimize Spark workloads with 40% better performance
  • Managed scaling analyzes executor utilization for automatic cluster sizing
  • Consider Savings Plans for predictable baseline capacity during business hours

questions.title: Data Classification and Discovery
questions.scenario: A healthcare company is migrating data to AWS and needs to discover and classify sensitive information including Protected Health Information (PHI), Social Security numbers, and credit card data across their S3 data lake. They require automated scanning, classification reports, and alerts when sensitive data is detected in unauthorized locations.
questions.questionText: Which service automates sensitive data discovery and classification?

choices.text: Amazon Inspector scanning S3 objects
AWS Config rules checking S3 bucket configurations
Manual review using S3 Inventory reports
Amazon Macie with custom data identifiers and automated discovery

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Scanning petabytes for unknown PII patterns requires more than regex. What approach scales for discovery across many buckets?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Amazon Macie provides automated sensitive data discovery. Macie uses machine learning and pattern matching to identify PHI, PII, financial data, and credentials in S3. Custom data identifiers extend detection to organization-specific patterns. Automated discovery jobs scan buckets on schedule. Findings include data location, type, and severity. EventBridge integration enables alerts when sensitive data appears in unauthorized buckets. AWS Config monitors configurations, not data content. Inspector focuses on vulnerabilities. Manual review doesn't scale.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Macie managed data identifiers cover 100+ sensitive data types globally
  • Custom data identifiers use regex patterns for organization-specific data
  • Allow lists reduce false positives for known safe patterns like test data
  • Automated discovery provides statistical sampling for cost-effective scanning
  • Security Hub integration aggregates Macie findings with other security alerts

questions.title: API Data Integration
questions.scenario: A marketing analytics company needs to ingest data from 30 different SaaS platforms (Salesforce, HubSpot, Google Analytics, etc.) into their data lake. Each API has different authentication methods, rate limits, and data formats. Ingestion should run daily with automatic retry on failures and schema change detection.
questions.questionText: Which approach provides the most maintainable solution for multi-source API ingestion?

choices.text: Single EMR cluster running custom Python scripts
Amazon AppFlow with scheduled flows for supported connectors
AWS Glue Python Shell jobs with requests library
Custom Lambda functions for each API with Step Functions orchestration

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Building and maintaining custom API connectors for each SaaS vendor is expensive. Is there a way to avoid that per-vendor work?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Amazon AppFlow provides managed SaaS data integration. AppFlow offers pre-built connectors for Salesforce, HubSpot, Google Analytics, and 50+ other platforms, handling authentication (OAuth, API keys), rate limiting, and pagination automatically. Scheduled flows run daily with automatic retry logic. Built-in data transformation and validation catches schema changes. Flow logs provide visibility into transfer status. This eliminates connector maintenance burden. Custom Lambda requires building and maintaining each integration. EMR adds unnecessary complexity. Glue Python Shell has limited connector support.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• AppFlow private flows use AWS PrivateLink for data transfer without internet exposure
  • Field mapping and transformation apply during transfer without additional processing
  • Incremental transfer tracks changes using source timestamps or watermarks
  • Custom connectors extend AppFlow for proprietary APIs using Connector SDK
  • EventBridge triggers enable downstream processing when flows complete

questions.title: Graph Database for Relationship Analytics
questions.scenario: A social media company needs to analyze user relationships, content sharing patterns, and influence networks. Queries include finding shortest paths between users, detecting communities, and identifying influential nodes. The graph has 100 million nodes and 1 billion edges. Query latency must be under 100 milliseconds for interactive features.
questions.questionText: Which database architecture supports these graph analytics requirements?

choices.text: Amazon Neptune with Gremlin queries and read replicas
Amazon DynamoDB with adjacency list pattern
Amazon DocumentDB with embedded relationship arrays
Amazon Redshift with recursive CTEs for graph traversal

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Traversing multi-hop relationships (friend-of-friend, etc.) is the core workload. Are relational joins efficient for that pattern?

hints.label: Complete Explanation

questions.title: Database Migration Strategy
questions.scenario: A company is migrating a 5 TB Oracle data warehouse to Amazon Redshift. The migration must complete within a 48-hour maintenance window with minimal downtime. After migration, ongoing changes must sync until cutover. Schema conversion is needed as Oracle uses PL/SQL procedures.
questions.questionText: Which migration approach meets these requirements?

choices.text: Oracle GoldenGate replication to Redshift
AWS SCT for schema conversion, DMS for full load and CDC, with Redshift as target
Manual schema recreation and data export/import via S3
AWS DataSync for database file transfer

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Migrating from Oracle to Redshift involves two problems: converting the schema and moving the data. Can both be solved together?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: AWS SCT and DMS together provide the complete migration solution. Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) converts Oracle schemas and PL/SQL to Redshift-compatible SQL, flagging manual conversion needs. DMS performs the 5 TB full load within the maintenance window using parallel threads. CDC (Change Data Capture) continues syncing changes after full load until cutover, minimizing downtime. DMS validates data integrity between source and target. Manual migration is error-prone and slow. GoldenGate doesn't target Redshift natively. DataSync is for file storage, not databases.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• SCT extension packs convert PL/SQL to AWS Lambda functions where direct conversion isn't possible
  • DMS parallel load with multiple tables maximizes throughput for large datasets
  • CDC uses Oracle LogMiner or Binary Reader for minimal source impact
  • DMS validation compares row counts and checksums between source and target
  • Consider DMS Serverless for automatic scaling during peak migration load

questions.title: Multi-Model Database Requirements
questions.scenario: A content management platform stores articles with rich metadata, user relationships, and access patterns including full-text search, graph traversals for recommendations, and key-value lookups for sessions. Currently using three separate databases, they want to consolidate to reduce operational complexity while maintaining performance.
questions.questionText: Which database architecture balances consolidation with performance requirements?

choices.text: Amazon Neptune for graph with OpenSearch for search and DynamoDB for key-value (keep separate)
Amazon DocumentDB with full-text search indexes and graph queries via aggregation
Single DynamoDB table with GSIs and OpenSearch integration
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pg_trgm for search, Apache AGE for graph, and caching layer

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider that specialized databases often outperform multi-model compromises for distinct access patterns.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Keeping specialized databases (Neptune, OpenSearch, DynamoDB) is actually optimal here despite seeming like more complexity. Each database excels at its pattern: Neptune provides native graph traversal for recommendations with millisecond latency, OpenSearch delivers full-text search with relevance ranking, and DynamoDB offers single-digit millisecond key-value access for sessions. Consolidation attempts compromise performance. DocumentDB graph queries don't match Neptune's efficiency. DynamoDB search requires OpenSearch anyway. PostgreSQL extensions add complexity without matching specialized performance.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Neptune's index-free adjacency makes multi-hop traversals O(1) per hop
  • OpenSearch relevance scoring (BM25) optimizes content search quality
  • DynamoDB DAX provides microsecond caching for session lookups
  • Data synchronization via DynamoDB Streams to Neptune and OpenSearch
  • Consider operational consolidation via infrastructure-as-code rather than database consolidation

questions.title: Resource Tagging Strategy
questions.scenario: A data platform spans multiple AWS accounts with resources including S3 buckets, Glue jobs, EMR clusters, and Redshift. Finance needs cost allocation by project and team. Operations needs to identify resource owners. Security needs to track data classification levels. Current tagging is inconsistent across teams.
questions.questionText: Which approach ensures consistent tagging across the data platform?

choices.text: Documentation requesting teams tag resources voluntarily
AWS Organizations Tag Policies with mandatory tags, enforced via Service Control Policies
Periodic manual audits of resource tags
Post-deployment Lambda functions adding missing tags

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Is it better to fix missing tags after the fact or prevent untagged resources from being created in the first place?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: AWS Organizations Tag Policies with SCP enforcement ensures consistent tagging. Tag Policies define mandatory tags (project, team, data-classification) and allowed values across the organization. SCPs can deny resource creation without required tags, preventing untagged resources. AWS Config rules detect and report non-compliant resources for remediation. Cost Explorer uses tags for accurate allocation. Resource Groups organize resources by tags for operations. Documentation alone leads to inconsistency. Manual audits are reactive. Post-deployment fixes allow gaps.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Tag Policies enforce tag key capitalization and allowed values organization-wide
  • SCP condition: "Condition": {"Null": {"aws:RequestTag/project": "true"}} denies untagged creation
  • AWS Config rule: required-tags checks existing resources for compliance
  • Cost Allocation Tags must be activated in Billing console for Cost Explorer
  • Tag Editor enables bulk tag updates across multiple resources and regions

questions.title: IAM Best Practices for Data Teams
questions.scenario: A data engineering team of 15 people needs access to Glue, S3, and Athena. Currently, all team members share a single IAM user with admin access. The security team requires individual accountability, least privilege access, and MFA enforcement. Some team members need read-only access while others need full development permissions.
questions.questionText: Which IAM structure implements security best practices?

choices.text: Continue sharing credentials with stronger password
Single IAM role assumed by all team members
Create 15 IAM users each with individual inline policies
Individual IAM users in groups (DataEngineers-ReadOnly, DataEngineers-Developer) with role-based policies and MFA requirement

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How do you balance individual accountability with manageable permission assignments for 15 people?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Individual IAM users in permission-based groups provides proper access control. Each team member has their own IAM user enabling individual accountability via CloudTrail logs. Groups (DataEngineers-ReadOnly, DataEngineers-Developer) apply appropriate permission policies based on job function. MFA is enforced via IAM policy conditions. This implements least privilege - read-only users can't modify resources. Managed policies attached to groups simplify administration. Shared credentials eliminate accountability. Individual inline policies are unmanageable. Single role lacks differentiated access.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• IAM policy condition: "Bool": {"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "true"} requires MFA
  • Permission boundaries limit maximum permissions even for administrators
  • AWS SSO with Identity Center provides centralized access with automatic MFA
  • CloudTrail logs show specific IAM user for each API call
  • Consider attribute-based access control (ABAC) for dynamic permissions based on tags

questions.title: Event-Driven Architecture for Data
questions.scenario: A supply chain platform needs to react to inventory events in real-time. When stock levels drop, purchasing workflows should trigger. When shipments arrive, warehouse systems should update. Events come from multiple sources (ERP, WMS, IoT sensors) in different formats. The architecture should be loosely coupled and scalable.
questions.questionText: Which architecture implements event-driven data processing?

choices.text: Amazon EventBridge with schema registry, rules routing to Lambda/Step Functions targets
Shared database with polling for changes
Message queue with single consumer processing all events
Direct point-to-point API integrations between systems

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Adding a new downstream system should not require changes to the upstream producer. What architectural pattern achieves that?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Amazon EventBridge provides enterprise event-driven architecture. EventBridge accepts events from multiple sources (custom applications, AWS services, SaaS partners) into a central bus. Schema registry discovers and validates event formats from different systems. Rules route events based on content (event type, attribute values) to appropriate targets. Lambda handles simple transformations while Step Functions orchestrate complex workflows. This decouples systems - producers don't know consumers. Point-to-point creates tight coupling. Database polling adds latency. Single consumer becomes a bottleneck.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• EventBridge rules use event patterns for content-based filtering (JSONPath-like)
  • Schema registry auto-discovers schemas from events for documentation
  • Archive and replay enables reprocessing historical events for recovery
  • Input transformers modify event payloads before delivery to targets
  • Cross-account event delivery enables organization-wide event mesh

questions.title: Search and Analytics Integration
questions.scenario: An e-commerce platform needs product search with faceted filtering, autocomplete suggestions, and relevance tuning based on sales data. Search results should incorporate real-time inventory status. The catalog contains 5 million products with 100 attributes each. Search latency must be under 200 milliseconds.
questions.questionText: Which search architecture meets these requirements?

choices.text: Relational database with full-text indexes
Amazon Kendra for enterprise search
Amazon OpenSearch with DynamoDB Streams for real-time inventory sync
ElastiCache with pre-computed search results

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Faceted search with filters across many dimensions is a specific workload. Is a general-purpose database the right fit for it?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Amazon OpenSearch provides the required search capabilities. OpenSearch supports faceted aggregations for filtering by category, brand, price ranges. Completion suggester enables fast autocomplete. Function score queries blend relevance with sales data for ranking. DynamoDB Streams with Lambda keeps inventory status synchronized in near real-time. OpenSearch handles 5M documents with sub-200ms latency on appropriately sized clusters. Relational databases don't scale for complex faceted search. Kendra is for document search, not product catalogs. Pre-computed results can't handle dynamic facet combinations.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• OpenSearch aggregations support nested facets (category > subcategory > brand)
  • Completion suggester uses FST (finite state transducer) for fast prefix matching
  • Function score: multiply(_score, log1p(sales_count)) boosts popular products
  • Index aliases enable zero-downtime reindexing for schema changes
  • UltraWarm nodes reduce storage costs for less frequently accessed products

questions.title: CI/CD for Data Infrastructure
questions.scenario: A data platform team manages 50+ Glue jobs, 20 Step Functions, and associated IAM roles across dev, staging, and production environments. Currently, infrastructure changes are manual and error-prone. The team wants infrastructure-as-code with automated testing and promotion between environments.
questions.questionText: Which approach implements CI/CD for data infrastructure?

choices.text: Shell scripts creating resources via AWS CLI
Manual CloudFormation template updates through console
AWS CDK with CodePipeline, environment-specific stacks, and integration tests
Terraform Cloud with separate state per resource

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: How do you promote infrastructure changes through dev, staging, and production with confidence and rollback capability?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: AWS CDK with CodePipeline provides comprehensive infrastructure CI/CD. CDK defines infrastructure in familiar programming languages (TypeScript, Python) with high-level constructs for Glue, Step Functions. Environment-specific stacks use CDK's stage concept for dev/staging/prod deployments. CodePipeline automates promotion: commit triggers build, unit tests validate constructs, deploy to dev, run integration tests, promote to staging/prod with approvals. CDK synth generates CloudFormation for drift detection. Manual templates don't scale with 50+ resources. CLI scripts lack state management. Terraform works but CDK has deeper AWS integration.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• CDK Pipelines construct simplifies multi-stage deployment with built-in best practices
  • CDK assertions library enables unit testing infrastructure constructs
  • CDK aspects apply cross-cutting concerns like tagging across all resources
  • Feature flags in CDK enable gradual rollout of infrastructure changes
  • CDK context values parameterize environment-specific configuration

questions.title: Data Retention and Deletion
questions.scenario: A company must implement data retention policies for GDPR compliance. Customer data must be deleted upon request within 30 days. Transaction records must be retained for 7 years for financial regulations. Some data spans multiple systems (S3, Redshift, DynamoDB). The deletion process must be auditable.
questions.questionText: Which approach implements compliant data retention and deletion?

choices.text: Manual deletion by administrators when requested
S3 Lifecycle policies for retention, Lambda orchestration for cross-system deletion with CloudTrail audit
Anonymization only without actual deletion
Single database with built-in retention policies

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider automated lifecycle management combined with orchestrated deletion workflows.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: S3 Lifecycle with Lambda orchestration provides compliant retention management. S3 Lifecycle rules automatically delete objects after 7 years or transition to Glacier for cost-effective retention. For deletion requests, Step Functions orchestrates deletion across S3, Redshift (DELETE queries), and DynamoDB (DeleteItem) with the customer identifier. Lambda functions execute deletions with error handling and retry logic. CloudTrail logs all delete operations for audit proof. DynamoDB TTL handles automatic expiration where applicable. Manual processes don't scale and lack audit trails. Single database doesn't reflect multi-system reality. Anonymization may not satisfy GDPR's right to erasure.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• S3 Object Lock compliance mode prevents deletion even by root for retention periods
  • Redshift DELETE with customer_id uses sort key for efficient targeted deletion
  • DynamoDB TTL automatically deletes expired items without provisioned capacity
  • Step Functions provides execution history as deletion audit trail
  • Consider data catalog tracking which systems contain each customer's data

questions.title: Message Queue Selection
questions.scenario: An order processing system needs to decouple order placement from fulfillment processing. Orders must be processed exactly once to prevent duplicate shipments. Processing can take up to 10 minutes per order. During peak sales, order volume increases 10x. The system should handle failures gracefully with retry capability.
questions.questionText: Which messaging service meets these requirements?

choices.text: Amazon SQS FIFO queue with visibility timeout and dead-letter queue
Amazon SNS for pub/sub notification
Amazon MQ with ActiveMQ
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Order processing cannot tolerate duplicates or reordering. What messaging guarantee does this workload require?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Amazon SQS FIFO queue provides exactly-once processing for order workflows. FIFO queues deduplicate messages within a 5-minute window preventing duplicate orders. Message group IDs ensure related messages process in order. Visibility timeout (set to 10+ minutes) prevents other consumers from processing during fulfillment. Dead-letter queues capture failed messages for investigation. SQS scales automatically with 10x traffic without configuration. SNS doesn't provide queuing. Amazon MQ requires capacity management. Kinesis is for streaming analytics, not work queues.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• FIFO deduplication uses message deduplication ID or content-based deduplication
  • Message group ID partitions messages for parallel processing with ordering
  • Visibility timeout should exceed maximum processing time plus buffer
  • Dead-letter queue maxReceiveCount configures retry attempts before DLQ
  • SQS FIFO supports 3,000 messages/second with batching (300 without)

questions.title: Real-Time Analytics Architecture
questions.scenario: A ride-sharing company needs real-time dashboards showing driver locations, trip counts by zone, and surge pricing recommendations. Data updates every second from 100,000 active drivers. Dashboards must refresh every 5 seconds with sub-second query latency. Historical analysis of patterns over months is also required.
questions.questionText: Which architecture supports both real-time dashboards and historical analysis?

choices.text: Kafka with consumer writing directly to dashboards
All data to Redshift with materialized views
Single PostgreSQL database for all queries
Kinesis Data Analytics for real-time aggregation to DynamoDB/ElastiCache, with Firehose to S3 for historical Athena queries

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider lambda architecture with real-time and batch layers serving different query patterns.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Kinesis Data Analytics with dual output paths serves both requirements. KDA (Apache Flink) processes streaming driver locations, computing real-time aggregations (trips per zone, driver density). Results write to DynamoDB or ElastiCache for sub-second dashboard queries. Simultaneously, Kinesis Firehose delivers raw data to S3 in Parquet format for historical analysis via Athena. This lambda architecture separates real-time serving from batch analytics. Redshift can't achieve 5-second refresh at this scale. PostgreSQL can't handle the write volume. Direct Kafka-to-dashboard lacks aggregation and persistence.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Flink tumbling windows aggregate trips per zone per 5-second intervals
  • ElastiCache provides microsecond read latency for dashboard queries
  • Firehose dynamic partitioning organizes S3 data by hour/zone for efficient queries
  • Consider Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink for fully managed streaming
  • Geospatial functions in Flink calculate zone membership from lat/long coordinates

questions.title: Performance Troubleshooting
questions.scenario: A Redshift cluster shows degraded query performance. Some queries that took 30 seconds now take 10 minutes. The cluster has grown from 500 GB to 5 TB over the past year. Disk usage is at 85%. Some tables haven't been vacuumed in months. The WLM shows queries waiting in queue.
questions.questionText: Which combination of actions addresses these performance issues?

choices.text: Create more WLM queues
Run VACUUM and ANALYZE on tables, resize cluster or enable concurrency scaling, review sort key effectiveness
Restart the cluster to clear memory
Delete old data to reduce disk usage

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Degraded performance after heavy writes often points to physical data organization. What routine maintenance addresses that?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: VACUUM, ANALYZE, and scaling address the performance issues systematically. VACUUM reclaims space from deleted rows and resorts data, critical for tables not maintained in months. ANALYZE updates statistics enabling the query planner to choose efficient execution plans. At 85% disk with 10x data growth, the cluster is undersized - resize to RA3 with managed storage or enable concurrency scaling for queue wait times. Review sort keys as data patterns may have changed. Restarting doesn't fix underlying issues. More WLM queues don't add capacity. Deleting data is a business decision, not a technical fix.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• VACUUM DELETE reclaims space; VACUUM SORT resorts rows for range queries
  • ANALYZE updates table statistics used by query planner for join strategies
  • Concurrency Scaling adds transient clusters for query queue overflow
  • STL_ALERT_EVENT_LOG shows inefficient queries needing optimization
  • SVV_TABLE_INFO shows vacuum status, sort percentage, and statistics staleness

questions.title: Zero Trust Data Access
questions.scenario: A financial institution is implementing zero trust security for their data platform. Every data access request must be verified regardless of network location. Access decisions should consider user identity, device posture, data sensitivity, and access patterns. Anomalous access should trigger additional verification or blocking.
questions.questionText: Which architecture implements zero trust data access?

choices.text: IP allowlisting in security groups
Shared service accounts with strong passwords
IAM Identity Center with MFA, Lake Formation permissions, Amazon Verified Access, and GuardDuty for anomaly detection
VPN with network-based access controls

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Zero trust means the network perimeter is not enough. What must be verified on every request instead?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: The combination of IAM Identity Center, Lake Formation, Verified Access, and GuardDuty implements zero trust principles. IAM Identity Center provides centralized identity with MFA for strong authentication regardless of network. Amazon Verified Access evaluates device posture and user context for application access decisions. Lake Formation enforces fine-grained data permissions based on identity and data sensitivity tags. GuardDuty detects anomalous access patterns (unusual data volumes, off-hours access) triggering alerts or blocking. This verifies every request. VPN trusts network location. IP allowlisting is perimeter-based. Shared accounts lack accountability.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Verified Access policies evaluate user groups, device trust, and request context
  • Lake Formation data filters restrict access based on user attributes (ABAC)
  • GuardDuty S3 protection detects unusual API calls and data access patterns
  • IAM Access Analyzer validates that policies don't grant unintended access
  • CloudWatch Logs Insights enables custom anomaly detection on access patterns

questions.title: Data Catalog Strategy
questions.scenario: A data platform contains 10,000 datasets across S3, Redshift, and RDS. Data consumers struggle to find relevant datasets. Metadata is inconsistent - some datasets have descriptions, others don't. Business users need to discover data using business terms while technical users need schema details. Data stewards need to maintain quality and documentation.
questions.questionText: Which approach creates a comprehensive data catalog?

choices.text: Documentation wiki maintained by data engineers
Spreadsheet tracking all datasets manually
Glue Data Catalog with crawlers only
Amazon DataZone with Glue Data Catalog integration, business glossary, and data quality rules

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Technical metadata alone does not help business users find data. What layer bridges the gap between schema and business meaning?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Amazon DataZone with Glue integration provides comprehensive cataloging. DataZone creates a business data catalog portal where data consumers search and discover datasets. Business glossary maps technical terms to business concepts (e.g., "customer_ltv" = "Customer Lifetime Value"). Glue Data Catalog provides technical metadata (schemas, statistics) via crawlers. Data stewards define ownership, maintain documentation, and set quality rules within DataZone. Self-service subscription enables governed data access. Spreadsheets don't scale. Glue alone lacks business context. Wikis become outdated.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• DataZone domains organize datasets by business area with dedicated governance
  • Data products package related datasets with documentation and quality SLAs
  • Business glossary inheritance applies terms to matching columns automatically
  • Subscription workflows enable data consumers to request access with approvals
  • DataZone integrates lineage from Glue showing data flow across transformations
